Step 2: Let the LLM Grade and Read the Agreement
~5 min | Goal: read how far your labels and the LLM’s judgments agree.
uv run python -m app.judge
• Calls the LLM once per item, 10 calls in total (about a minute). If “Rate limit reached” appears, wait one minute and run again.
• If you cannot use an API key, add --model test to try only the workflow without calling the API (this is not real grading).
How to read the output
• Agreement by criterion: which criteria disagree.
• Overall agreement and coverage: the proportion that could be judged automatically.
• Needs review: items the LLM marked unsure, with reasons.
• Breakdown of disagreements: misses (LLM=pass, you=fail) / false alarms (the reverse).
Example output (run with --model test; the numbers differ from actual model grading)
Agreement by criterion (your labels versus LLM judgments, 10 cases)
  Grounding              8/9    Needs review: 1
  Scope                 10/10
  Hint                  10/10
  Clarity                9/10
  Lecture marker (code) 10/10
Overall agreement   8/9   (Automatically judged 9/10 cases = coverage 90%)
Needs review: 1 item (the LLM marked unsure; a person reviews it)
  #05 Grounding: The answer gives a general explanation after stating that the term is not in the glossary,
                 so it falls under “Unresolved Questions”.
Disagreements: 2 items
  #09 Clarity    Miss (LLM=pass, you=fail)         Reason: …
  #10 Grounding  False alarm (LLM=fail, you=pass)  Reason: …
→ Saved to lectures/04/judge_result.json
Reading order: first check the low agreement for Clarity. Subjective criteria divide people too.
Next, look at the items needing review. Step 3 addresses these.

corrections.after:
Step 3: Fix One Thing in the Criteria and Grade Again
~8 min | Goal: decide a policy for an item needing review, revise rubric.md, run again, and record the change.
1. Look at items needing review: the “Needs review” section in Step 2 lists the items the LLM marked unsure and their reasons. If there are none, choose an item you marked “Unsure”.
2. Revise rubric.md: decide for yourself whether the item should pass or fail. Add one or two lines under the relevant criterion and remove the issue from “Unresolved Questions” (example below).
3. Run again and record: run uv run python -m app.judge again, then write the change in the number of items needing review and the item’s judgment in lectures/04/answer.md.
Example revision: #05 “What is RAG?” needed review because the answer gave a general explanation of a term after stating that it is absent from the glossary.
Before: data/eval/rubric.md (excerpt)
## Grounding (grounding)
- Statements about information in the glossary do not contradict the referenced glossary entries.
- For information absent from the glossary, the answer states that it is not in the glossary instead of asserting guesses.
## Unresolved Questions (choose unsure for answers covered here)
- Whether giving a general explanation of a term after stating that it is absent from the glossary counts as “asserting guesses”.
After (policy: not an unsupported assertion → pass)
## Grounding (grounding)
- Statements about information in the glossary do not contradict the referenced glossary entries.
- For information absent from the glossary, the answer states that it is not in the glossary instead of asserting guesses.
- Giving a general explanation of a term after stating that it is absent from the glossary is not an unsupported assertion (pass).  ← Add this.
## Unresolved Questions (choose unsure for answers covered here)
  ← Remove the line about this issue.
Running again changes the number of items needing review from 1 → 0, and #05 Grounding becomes pass. If you chose a fail policy, add this complete line instead: “Giving a general explanation of a term after stating that it is absent from the glossary counts as an unsupported assertion (fail).” The result then becomes fail.
corrections.reason: Translate both complete previously Japanese-only rubric excerpts, keeping the grounding key, pass/fail/unsure values and the exact source before/after workflow. Use reviewed terminology from the published English rubric; retain the alternative fail policy and the zero-review fallback, not only the successful pass example. Expand the source’s abbreviated alternative into a complete one-line general explanation … (fail) policy so copying it into the rubric matches the existing English test grader’s general.*\(fail\) pattern; no policy choice is changed.
